title: Episode 236: Switzerland: William Tell, the Apple Shot at Altdorf, and the Oath of the Rütli
description:
The legendary birth of Swiss liberty in 1307: the heroic mountaineer William Tell defying the tyrannical Habsburg bailiff Gessler, shooting the apple off his son's head, and the eternal Oath of the Rütli.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, we journey into the towering, snow-capped granite peaks and emerald valleys of the central Alps to follow the immortal legend that forged the soul of the Swiss nation: William Tell, the apple shot at Altdorf, and the Oath of the Rütli.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ALPINE VALLEYS AND THE HABSBURG YOKE
In the late thirteenth century, the soaring peaks, deep glacial gorges, and pristine blue waters of Lake Lucerne in central Switzerland were inhabited by independent mountain communities of free cattle farmers, hunters, and woodsmen in the three forest cantons: Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden. For generations, these hardy alpine villagers had enjoyed direct imperial immediacy under the Holy Roman Empire, governing their communities through the Landsgemeinde—open-air democratic assemblies where every free peasant raised his right hand to vote on communal laws, pastures, and forestry rights. But with the rise of the powerful House of Habsburg, the Austrian dukes sought to extinguish local autonomy and incorporate the strategic Gotthard mountain pass into their feudal empire. Habsburg bailiffs, known as Landvögte, were dispatched into the valleys to impose heavy feudal taxes, seize communal grazing lands, and enforce arbitrary Austrian justice, breeding simmering resentment among the fiercely independent mountaineers.  In the forest cantons, every alpine family was self-sufficient, raising hardy brown Simmental cattle, churning cheese in high summer pastures, and cutting hay on steep mountain slopes using handheld scythes.  The mountain cantons maintained intricate customary laws governing the seasonal migration of cattle to high alpine pastures, using carved wooden tallies to record grazing rights and shared cheese production.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE OATH OF THE RÜTLI: AUGUST 1, 1291
Following the death of King Rudolf of Habsburg in 1291, leaders from the three forest cantons gathered in absolute secrecy in the dead of night on the Rütli meadow—a hidden, forested terrace overlooking the dark waters of Lake Lucerne. Led by Werner Stauffacher of Schwyz, Walter Fürst of Uri, and Arnold von Melchtal of Unterwalden, thirty-three representatives joined hands beneath the starry alpine heavens and swore a solemn, binding covenant: the Federal Charter of 1291, the founding document of the Swiss Confederation. In an era of feudal servitude, these humble alpine peasants pledged mutual defensive assistance against all external oppressors, declaring that an attack on one canton was an attack on all. They resolved that they would never accept foreign judges or hereditary overlords in their valleys, establishing a confederation built not on royal blood or imperial decrees, but on fraternal solidarity, mutual defense, and unyielding local democracy, a date celebrated today as Swiss National Day.  The Federal Charter of 1291 was written in concise, formal Latin on a single sheet of vellum, sealed with the wax seals of Uri and Schwyz, and kept in a secret iron-bound chest in the town archives of Schwyz.  The Rütli meadow remains a revered national sanctuary where generations of Swiss citizens gather to reaffirm their devotion to federal unity, constitutional democracy, and shared mutual responsibility.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE TYRANT GESSLER AND THE HAT ON THE POLE
Into this tense alpine crucible stepped Albrecht Gessler, the cruel and arrogant Habsburg bailiff of Altdorf in Uri. Determined to break the proud spirit of the Swiss peasantry and test their obedience to the Austrian crown, Gessler erected a tall wooden pole in the center of the main market square of Altdorf, perched his feathered Habsburg ducal hat upon the top, and posted armed guards beside it. He issued a royal proclamation commanding every citizen who passed through the square to bow their heads and kneel before the hat in reverence, under pain of death and confiscation of all property. The humiliated townspeople bowed sullenly as they walked past, but one man refused: William Tell of Bürglen, a renowned mountain huntsman celebrated across the canton for his quiet dignity, peerless physical strength, and legendary marksmanship with the crossbow.  Gessler had built a formidable stone fortress overlooking the village of Altdorf, stationing mercenary crossbowmen and tax collectors who harassed travelers along the Gotthard trade route.  Gessler's ducal hat was crafted from green velvet adorned with peacock feathers, an imperial Habsburg symbol meant to remind the proud Swiss that their alpine valleys belonged to the Austrian crown.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE APPLE SHOT AT ALTDORF: NOVEMBER 18, 1307
On November 18, 1307, William Tell walked into the square of Altdorf holding the hand of his young son, Walter. Walking straight past the pole, Tell held his head high and refused to bow before the bailiff's hat. Gessler's guards seized him immediately and dragged him before the bailiff. Gessler was filled with malicious fury: learning of Tell's famed marksmanship, the tyrant devised a sadistic, horrifying punishment. He commanded Tell to place an apple upon the head of his young son, stand at a distance of eighty paces, and split the fruit with a single crossbow bolt. If Tell succeeded, his life would be spared; if he refused or missed, both father and son would be executed immediately. Tell fell to his knees, begging Gessler to kill him rather than force him to risk the life of his beloved child. But young Walter encouraged his father, crying out proudly: 'I am not afraid! My father can hit a bird on the wing at a hundred yards; shoot, father, I will not flinch!' With a weeping crowd holding its breath, Tell loaded his bow, aimed with iron concentration, and loosed the bolt. The arrow whistled through the air, splitting the apple squarely in half without touching a single hair on the boy's head.  Young Walter's fearless courage was remembered across Switzerland as the true heart of the legend, inspiring generations of Swiss schoolchildren with the noble words: 'Shoot, father, I will not flinch!'  When William Tell embraced his son after the shot, tears of relief streamed down his cheeks as the boy handed him the split halves of the apple, smiling proudly at his father's peerless skill.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SECOND BOLT: TELL'S DEFIANT CONFESSION
The square erupted in ecstatic cheers of relief, but Gessler's sharp eyes noticed that as Tell had prepared his bow, he had tucked a second crossbow bolt into his leather jerkin. 'Tell,' the bailiff demanded with a cold sneer, 'why did you conceal a second bolt within your clothes, since I granted you but a single shot?' Tell looked Gessler directly in the eyes with unflinching courage and answered with words that echoed across the centuries: 'Noble bailiff, since you demand the truth, I will speak it: had my first arrow struck my dear child, this second bolt was intended for your heart, and rest assured, I would not have missed.' Enraged by Tell's insolence, Gessler shouted that although he had promised Tell his life, he had not promised him his liberty. He ordered Tell bound in heavy iron chains and dragged aboard the bailiff's royal ship to be transported across Lake Lucerne to the dungeon fortress of Küssnacht, where Tell would spend the remainder of his life in dark chains.  Tell's defiant answer to Gessler became a timeless manifesto of personal liberty, proving that an upright and honorable man cannot be compelled to surrender his conscience to arbitrary political tyranny.  Tell's refusal to compromise his dignity before the tyrannical bailiff embodied the ancient Germanic legal principle that an unjust ruler forfeits his moral right to the obedience of free men.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE FÖHN STORM AND THE LEAP AT THE AXEN
As Gessler's boat sailed across Lake Lucerne, a terrifying alpine gale known as the Föhn erupted through the narrow mountain gorges, whipping the deep lake into churning twenty-foot waves that threatened to capsize the vessel against the sheer granite cliffs of the Axen mountain. Terrified that the boat would be lost, the Austrian oarsmen reminded Gessler that Tell was the most skilled steersman on the lake and begged that his chains be removed so he could save them. Gessler ordered Tell's irons struck off. Grasping the heavy steering oar, Tell skillfully guided the boat through the breaking surf toward a flat shelf of rock jutting from the cliffs. As the bow brushed the ledge, Tell seized his beloved crossbow, leaped onto the rock shelf—known to this day as the Tellsplatte—and kicked the boat backward into the stormy waves with his boots. Tell scaled the jagged cliffs, vanishing into the mountain forests, while Gessler and his men fought their way ashore.  The rock shelf of the Tellsplatte remains one of the most sacred national pilgrimage sites in Switzerland, where a peaceful memorial chapel adorned with historic frescoes overlooks the deep blue waters of Lake Lucerne.  The Tellsplatte chapel contains four monumental frescoes painted by Ernst Stückelberg, depicting the apple shot, the leap from the boat, Gessler's assassination, and the oath at the Rütli.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE HOLLOW WAY AND THE SPARK OF SWISS FREEDOM
Tell ran through the forests to the sunken road between Immensee and Küssnacht, known as the Hohle Gasse—the 'Hollow Way'—an overgrown ravine through which Gessler would have to pass to reach his castle. Concealed behind a thick elder bush, Tell waited with his crossbow loaded. As Gessler and his armed escort rode into the ravine, cursing the escaped rebel, Tell released his second bolt. The arrow struck Gessler through the heart, killing the tyrant on the spot. Tell's bold act of resistance became the spark that ignited the general uprising across the forest cantons: Swiss patriots stormed Habsburg castles, tore down royal fortresses, and drove Austrian bailiffs from the valleys forever. At the Battle of Morgarten in 1315 and Sempach in 1386, Swiss halberdiers crushed heavily armored Austrian knightly armies, proving that free citizen-soldiers defending their homeland could defeat any imperial army. Whether historical fact or founding legend, William Tell stands as the eternal symbol of individual courage, human dignity, and the unyielding spirit of Swiss independence.  At Morgarten in 1315, Swiss mountaineers concealed on the forested heights rolled massive boulders and tree trunks down onto the Austrian knightly cavalry, turning the narrow pass into an inescapable deathtrap.  The Swiss victories at Morgarten and Sempach demonstrated that tightly disciplined infantry armed with polearms could decisively break the cavalry shock of feudal chivalry, transforming European military tactics.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our European journey concludes with our final epic episode: Episode 237: Switzerland Part 2—Armed Neutrality, the Red Cross of Henri Dunant, and the Alpine Redoubt. Until then, stay curious.
